digest_preimages.rfc_expectation_digest: CORRECTED BASIS. Sections 4.1 and 4.2.1 govern the client's generation of the opening handshake and the server's reading and validation of it. Neither says anything about line terminators, so the governing rule is HTTP's, and the superseded record read it backwards. RFC 9112 section 2.2 reads, verbatim: "Although the line terminator for the start-line and fields is the sequence CRLF, a recipient MAY recognize a single LF as a line terminator and ignore any preceding CR." That is a MAY, addressed to the RECIPIENT. It permits recognizing a bare LF; it does not require it, and it does not make a message containing one malformed. A recipient that declines the MAY does not refuse the message either: no line ever terminates at that point, so the bare LF is an ordinary content byte and the surviving CRLF-terminated lines decide the observable. Both behaviours conform, so RFC 6455 and RFC 9112 together leave this observable undetermined.
digest_preimages.rfc_value_digest: recipient-choice: RFC 9112 section 2.2 permits but does not require recognizing a bare LF as a line terminator, so folding the bare-LF line into the next and refusing the message are both conformant

finding.the_contradiction: Sequence 13 rfc_expectation: "RFC 9112 section 2.2 terminates lines with CRLF and forbids a bare LF as a line terminator, so the message is malformed and must be refused." Sequence 39 rfc_expectation: "RFC 9112 section 2.2 makes bare-LF handling a RECIPIENT CHOICE, not a rejection requirement." Both are inside their records' digest preimages, so neither can be edited; the later one is right.

proposed_definition.Rationale: SUPERSEDING CORRECTION for ledger sequence 13 (delta-5084efaf08126e24d74a1bdea7da8b88eca6ef69fce631aef388c61ea3a86db2, subject semantic:org.java-websocket.draft6455.server-handshake.bare-lf.hs0034:provisional-v1). THE SUPERSEDED RECORD'S BASIS WAS WRONG, and the chain already contains the reading that shows it. Sequence 13 bound, verbatim: "RFC 9112 section 2.2 terminates lines with CRLF and forbids a bare LF as a line terminator, so the message is malformed and must be refused." Section 2.2 does not forbid it. It reads "a recipient MAY recognize a single LF as a line terminator", which PERMITS the recognition and imposes nothing on a recipient that declines it. Sequence 39, appended later for the CLIENT direction of the same clause, states the correction in as many words -- "THE NORMATIVE POSITION IS NARROWER THAN AN EARLIER DRAFT OF THIS RECORD CLAIMED" -- but corrected only its own direction, leaving the server-direction record at sequence 13 standing on the refuted reading. This is the same defect sequences 45-47 corrected for the section 10.4 basis: a normative premise nobody re-checked after it was found wrong elsewhere. WHAT CHANGES AS A RESULT: the superseded record is classed as a leniency divergence, as though shipped Java were failing an RFC requirement. It is not. Since the RFC leaves bare-LF recognition to the recipient, what is recorded is a MODEL-versus-JAVA divergence at a point the RFC does not determine, plus the genuine field-value consequence the mid-message fold produces. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: the recorded Java behaviour, the live evidence, the corpus case and the port's behaviour are all exactly as the superseded record described. WS_CORE SITE: rust/ws-core/src/handshake/server.rs over rust/ws-core/src/handshake/http.rs (parse_java_head) reproduces the fold exactly; pinned by rust/ws-core/tests/handshake_server.rs::bare_lf_folds_into_the_next_line_and_still_accepts. SCOPE NOTE: this record corrects the NORMATIVE BASIS only. It does not withdraw the superseded record, which remains in the chain at sequence 13 with its digest intact. AUTOBAHN: leg not executed (baseline BLOCKED 0/247, NO_FURTHER_RERUNS_AUTHORIZED); refs are nominal anchors.

why_this_is_a_draft_and_not_an_append: This branch appends nothing to the ledger. The finding is that ledger sequence 13's sealed rfc_expectation reads RFC 9112 section 2.2 as FORBIDDING a bare LF, while sequence 39 -- appended later, about the same clause on the client direction -- reads it correctly as a recipient MAY and says so explicitly. Sequence 13 was never revisited, so the chain carries both readings of one clause. Sealed records are never edited, so the remedy is a superseding record in the shape of sequences 45-47, and appending it is an owner decision.
